payload.set_intro:
Historical source (real document)
These sources are real historical sources (excerpts are cut verbatim from the repository text, with any OCR corrections listed in the credit line; [...] marks an omission).

Source A (secondary source)
Reconstruction, Political and Economic, 1865-1877 (excerpt on the Freedmen's Bureau)
William Archibald Dunning (Professor of History and Political Philosophy, Columbia University), 1907 (The American Nation: A History, vol. 22; Harper & Brothers; excerpts from pp. 32 and 34). Internet Archive (scan of the 1907 first edition, Trent University Library copy; item reconstructionpo0022dunn). Reuse: public domain in the United States (published before 1929). excerpted (two passages, p. 32 and p. 34, joined by [...]); whitespace normalized; OCR corrections only: 'r6le' to 'rôle', and line-break hyphenations 'judg¬ ment' and 'oppres¬ sive' rejoined; no other wording changed.
Context: From a volume on Reconstruction published in 1907 by a Columbia University historian. Dunning's account reflects the racial prejudices of its time and has since been widely criticized by historians.

"The bureau assumed, in short, a general guardianship of the emancipated race, and, backed by the paramount military force of the United States, undertook to play a determining rôle in the process of reorganizing southern society. The orders and instructions issued by General Howard, the head of the bureau, for carrying out this comprehensive programme, were characterized almost uniformly by moderation and good judgment. [...] Hence the working of the bureau, with its intrusion into the fundamental relationships of social life, engendered violent hostility from the outset on the part of the whites. The feeling was enhanced by the conduct of the ignorant, unscrupulous, and deliberately oppressive agents who were not rare. As soon, therefore, as it became established, the bureau took the form, to the southern mind, of a diabolical device for the perpetuation of the national government’s control over the South, and for the humiliation of the whites before their former slaves."

———

Source B (secondary source)
Reconstruction and Its Benefits (excerpt on the Freedmen's Bureau)
W. E. Burghardt Du Bois (Atlanta University); paper read at the American Historical Association, December 1909, 1910 (American Historical Review, vol. 15, July 1910, pp. 781-799; excerpts from p. 782 and p. 783). Internet Archive (JSTOR Early Journal Content, item jstor-1836959). Reuse: public domain in the United States (published before 1929). excerpted (two passages in their original order, p. 782 then p. 783, joined by [...]); whitespace normalized; line-break hyphenations 'educa- tional', 'gov- ernment', 'physi- cally' and 'social- istic' rejoined; no other wording changed.
Context: From an article by a Black historian and sociologist with a Harvard doctorate, presented to the American Historical Association in December 1909 and published in 1910. It was an early challenge to the then-dominant view of Reconstruction taught by Dunning and his students.

"It must not be forgotten that among the agents of the Freedmen's Bureau were not only soldiers and politicians but school-teachers and educational leaders like Ware and Cravath. [...] The Freedmen's Bureau was an attempt to establish a government guardianship over the negroes and insure their economic and civil rights. Its establishment was a herculean task both physically and socially, and it not only met the solid opposition of the white South, but even the North looked at the new thing as socialistic and over-paternal. It accomplished a great task but it was repudiated."

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Briefly describe ONE major difference between Dunning's and Du Bois's interpretations of the Freedmen's Bureau.
parts.model_answer: Dunning emphasizes that the Bureau's intrusion into Southern social life aroused violent hostility among white Southerners, while Du Bois emphasizes that it was an attempt to protect freed people's economic and civil rights.

rubric_rows.criterion: Describe one accurate difference between the two excerpts. Acceptable differences include: Dunning stresses the Bureau's intrusion into Southern social life and the hostility it aroused among white Southerners, while Du Bois stresses the Bureau's task of protecting freed people's economic and civil rights; Dunning faults the Bureau's local agents, while Du Bois credits Bureau agents who were teachers and educators; Dunning describes the Bureau as it appeared to the white South, while Du Bois judges that it accomplished a great task but was repudiated.
required_elements: Dunning emphasizes that the Bureau's intrusion into Southern social life aroused violent hostility among white Southerners, while Du Bois emphasizes that it was an attempt to protect freed people's economic and civil rights.
Dunning points to ignorant or oppressive local agents, while Du Bois points to Bureau agents who were teachers and educational leaders.
Dunning describes how the Bureau looked to the white South (a device for humiliating whites), while Du Bois judges that the Bureau accomplished a great task and was repudiated.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Briefly explain how ONE specific historical event or development from 1865 to 1877 that is not mentioned in the excerpts supports Dunning's interpretation.
parts.model_answer: Andrew Johnson vetoed the Freedmen's Bureau Bill on February 19, 1866, objecting that it would extend military jurisdiction over civilians in peacetime, with agents acting as judges without juries, in states that had no representation in Congress; this shows a contemporary view that the Bureau intruded into Southern life, which fits Dunning's claim.

rubric_rows.criterion: Credit requires BOTH (a) one specific, accurate event or development from 1865 to 1877 that the excerpts do not mention (what happened, who acted, roughly when) AND (b) an explicit explanation of how that fact supports Dunning's interpretation: the Bureau's intrusion into Southern life, the white hostility it provoked, its agents' conduct, or its role as an instrument of national control. A response that only repeats an event or claim already in the Dunning excerpt (for example that white Southerners resented the Bureau, that some local agents were oppressive, or that the Bureau intruded into social life) earns 0, even if it is true. A response that adds a specific outside fact and explains its connection may earn 1. Examples with the connection each needs (not an exhaustive list): (1) President Andrew Johnson's veto of the Freedmen's Bureau Bill on February 19, 1866: his veto message objected that the bill would extend military jurisdiction over civilians in peacetime, with Bureau agents acting as judges without juries, in eleven states that had no representation in Congress; the response must tie this objection to Dunning's claim that the Bureau intruded into Southern life and met opposition (the veto was one opponent's largely constitutional argument, so it supports the 'intrusion' claim, not Dunning's description of white feeling). (2) The Steedman-Fullerton inspection of 1866: Johnson sent Generals James Steedman and Joseph Fullerton to inspect the Bureau in the South (instructions of April 7, first report May 8, 1866); they reported that many agents interfered 'arbitrarily' in planter-laborer relations and sat in freedmen's courts deciding land and family disputes, that some officers competed with planters by running plantations and sawmills, and that this produced bitterness between whites and freedpeople, and they recommended transferring Bureau duties to the army; the response must tie these reported agent practices and resentment to Dunning's claims about oppressive agents and white hostility (limits: Johnson, an opponent of the Bureau, appointed the commissioners and later historians describe the inquiry as meant to discredit the Bureau; the same report praised 'judicious' officers and found good order where agents did not interfere; do not credit a response that says the report condemned the whole Bureau or proved Dunning's 'diabolical device' description). (3) The Bureau's role in Black voting in 1867: after the Military Reconstruction Acts of March 1867 required Southern states to elect constitutional conventions with Black men voting, Bureau Circular No. 9 (May 1, 1867) said measures would be taken to inform freedmen entitled to register and urged them to disregard threats; the response must tie the Bureau's involvement in Black registration and voting to Dunning's claim that white Southerners saw the Bureau as an instrument of national control (limit: army commanders, not the Bureau, ran registration; do not credit a response that says Bureau agents registered the voters or ran the elections). Other accurate events or developments from 1865 to 1877 are accepted when they are specific, verifiable, not in the excerpt, and linked to Dunning's claim by the response's own explanation. Naming an event without connecting it to the interpretation earns 0.
required_elements: Andrew Johnson vetoed the Freedmen's Bureau Bill on February 19, 1866, objecting that it would extend military jurisdiction over civilians in peacetime, with agents acting as judges without juries, in states that had no representation in Congress; this shows a contemporary view that the Bureau intruded into Southern life, which fits Dunning's claim.

In 1866 Generals Steedman and Fullerton, sent by President Johnson, reported that many Bureau agents interfered arbitrarily in relations between planters and laborers and that this bred bitterness between whites and freedpeople; this documents the agent conduct and hostility Dunning describes (though the inquiry was appointed by an opponent of the Bureau).

After Congress required Black men to vote in the constitutional conventions of 1867, the Bureau (Circular No. 9, May 1867) told freedmen how to register and to disregard threats; white Southerners who saw the Bureau backing Black voters could read it as an instrument of national political control, as Dunning says.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Briefly explain how ONE specific historical event or development from 1865 to 1877 that is not mentioned in the excerpts supports Du Bois's interpretation.
parts.model_answer: In late 1865 Southern legislatures such as Mississippi's and South Carolina's passed Black Codes that required freed workers to hold yearly written labor contracts and punished those without lawful employment as vagrants, which shows the need for the protection of economic and civil rights that Du Bois says the Bureau attempted.

rubric_rows.criterion: Credit requires BOTH (a) one specific, accurate event or development from 1865 to 1877 that the excerpts do not mention (what happened, who acted, roughly when) AND (b) an explicit explanation of how that fact supports Du Bois's interpretation: the Bureau as an attempt to protect freed people's economic and civil rights, a great task accomplished, and a task repudiated. A response that only repeats what the Du Bois excerpt already says (that the Bureau met white opposition, that it was repudiated, or that its agents included teachers) earns 0; naming an event without explaining the link earns 0; adding a specific outside fact and explaining the link may earn 1. Examples with the connection each needs (not an exhaustive list): (1) The Black Codes of 1865-1866: in late 1865 legislatures such as Mississippi's and South Carolina's passed laws requiring freed workers to hold written yearly labor contracts, treating those without lawful employment as vagrants who could be fined and hired out, and restricting their rights in other ways; the response must tie the codes to the economic and civil rights Du Bois says the Bureau was meant to protect (limit: the codes show the need for protection, not that the Bureau succeeded). (2) Johnson's reversal of land policy, 1865-1866: Sherman's Special Field Order No. 15 (January 1865) had set aside coastal land in South Carolina and Georgia for freed families; after Johnson's amnesty and pardons, most of it, including land on Edisto Island, South Carolina, was returned to former owners in 1865-1866; the response must tie this to the national government's withdrawal of support for freed people's economic independence and so to Du Bois's judgment that the Bureau's work was repudiated (limit: Bureau officers themselves carried out the restoration; do not credit a response that says the Bureau opposed it). (3) Bureau support for Black colleges, credited only with an accurate role: the Fisk Free Colored School opened in Nashville in January 1866, founded by American Missionary Association representatives together with Bureau education superintendent John Ogden, and General Clinton B. Fisk helped secure former Union army hospital barracks for it; Howard University was chartered by Congress on March 2, 1867, was named for Bureau Commissioner O. O. Howard, who was one of its founders, and the Bureau helped fund its early campus (including a medical building and hospital in 1869); the response must tie the support to Du Bois's claim that the Bureau accomplished a great task (limits: do not credit a response that says the Bureau founded either college alone; the Du Bois excerpt already names Bureau teachers and educational leaders, so a general reference to Bureau schools, or to Cravath, earns 0). (4) The end of the Bureau: most of its work ended by 1868-1869 and Congress discontinued its remaining functions in 1872, while the rights of freed people were still contested; the response must tie this to Du Bois's judgment that the Bureau was repudiated (the end of the Bureau alone is not evidence that its work was a success). Other accurate events or developments from 1865 to 1877 are accepted when they are specific, verifiable, not in the excerpts, and linked to Du Bois's claim by the response's own explanation.
required_elements: In late 1865 Southern legislatures such as Mississippi's and South Carolina's passed Black Codes that required freed workers to hold yearly written labor contracts and punished those without lawful employment as vagrants, which shows the need for the protection of economic and civil rights that Du Bois says the Bureau attempted.

In 1865 and 1866 President Johnson's amnesty and pardons led to the return of most of the land that Sherman's Field Order No. 15 had set aside for freed families, including land on Edisto Island, South Carolina; the national government's withdrawal of support for freed families' economic independence supports Du Bois's point that the Bureau's task was repudiated.

Howard University was chartered by Congress in 1867 and named for Bureau Commissioner O. O. Howard, and the Bureau helped fund its early campus; Bureau support for such institutions supports Du Bois's statement that the Bureau accomplished a great task.

Most of the Bureau's work had ended by 1868-1869 and Congress discontinued its remaining functions in 1872, while freed people's rights were still contested, which supports Du Bois's statement that the Bureau was repudiated.

Sample response, high score (3/3; Part A 1, Part B 1, Part C 1):
(A) Dunning and Du Bois describe the Bureau from opposite points of view. Dunning stresses how the Bureau's reach into Southern social life made white Southerners hostile and treats many local agents as unfit, while Du Bois treats the Bureau as a great task meant to protect freed people's economic and civil rights that the country abandoned too soon.

(B) One development that supports Dunning is President Andrew Johnson's veto of the Freedmen's Bureau Bill on February 19, 1866. In his veto message Johnson objected that the bill would extend military jurisdiction over civilians in peacetime, with Bureau agents acting as judges without juries, in states that had no representatives in Congress. Legislatures such as Mississippi's and South Carolina's required freed workers to hold written yearly labor contracts and treated those without lawful employment as vagrants who could be fined and hired out. These laws threatened the economic and civil rights that Du Bois says the Bureau was meant to guarantee, so they show why the protection he describes was needed.

   - "which fits Dunning's claim that its working intruded into Southern society and aroused opposition" - Adds an outside fact (the contents of the veto message) and explains how it fits Dunning's claim, as the question requires. Earns the Part B point.
   - "treated those without lawful employment as vagrants who could be fined and hired out" - Accurate, specific detail about the Black Codes.
   - "so they show why the protection he describes was needed" - Explains how the Black Codes support Du Bois's view of the Bureau's purpose. Earns the Part C point.

(A) Dunning thinks the Freedmen's Bureau caused hostility among white Southerners, but Du Bois thinks it was a good attempt to protect the rights of freed people.

(B) Many white Southerners did not like the Bureau and resisted its agents. This supports Dunning because he says the Bureau caused violent hostility among the whites.

(C) The Black Codes passed by Southern states in late 1865 limited what freed people could do. Many codes required freed people to have a job and treated those who did not as vagrants, so freed people needed the Bureau to protect their rights, which is what Du Bois says.
   - "Dunning thinks the Freedmen's Bureau caused hostility among white Southerners" - Accurate contrast with Du Bois's view of the Bureau's purpose. Earns the Part A point.

   - "freed people needed the Bureau to protect their rights, which is what Du Bois says" - Connects the codes to Du Bois's interpretation. Earns the Part C point.

(A) Dunning and Du Bois both write about the Freedmen's Bureau, but Dunning says that white Southerners hated it and Du Bois says it did a great task.

descriptors.1: The response accurately describes a difference between the two authors' interpretations of the Bureau.

rows.task_specific: Describe one accurate difference between the two excerpts. Acceptable differences include: Dunning stresses the Bureau's intrusion into Southern social life and the hostility it aroused among white Southerners, while Du Bois stresses the Bureau's task of protecting freed people's economic and civil rights; Dunning faults the Bureau's local agents, while Du Bois credits Bureau agents who were teachers and educators; Dunning describes the Bureau as it appeared to the white South, while Du Bois judges that it accomplished a great task but was repudiated.

rows.name: Part B

descriptors.0: The response gives no event, an inaccurate or out-of-period event, only repeats an event or claim already in the Dunning excerpt, names an event without explaining how it supports Dunning, or adds an outside fact that does not bear on his interpretation.
descriptors.1: The response adds a specific, accurate event or development from 1865 to 1877 that is not in the excerpts and explains how it supports Dunning's interpretation.

rows.task_specific: Credit requires BOTH (a) one specific, accurate event or development from 1865 to 1877 that the excerpts do not mention (what happened, who acted, roughly when) AND (b) an explicit explanation of how that fact supports Dunning's interpretation: the Bureau's intrusion into Southern life, the white hostility it provoked, its agents' conduct, or its role as an instrument of national control. A response that only repeats an event or claim already in the Dunning excerpt (for example that white Southerners resented the Bureau, that some local agents were oppressive, or that the Bureau intruded into social life) earns 0, even if it is true. A response that adds a specific outside fact and explains its connection may earn 1. Examples with the connection each needs (not an exhaustive list): (1) President Andrew Johnson's veto of the Freedmen's Bureau Bill on February 19, 1866: his veto message objected that the bill would extend military jurisdiction over civilians in peacetime, with Bureau agents acting as judges without juries, in eleven states that had no representation in Congress; the response must tie this objection to Dunning's claim that the Bureau intruded into Southern life and met opposition (the veto was one opponent's largely constitutional argument, so it supports the 'intrusion' claim, not Dunning's description of white feeling). (2) The Steedman-Fullerton inspection of 1866: Johnson sent Generals James Steedman and Joseph Fullerton to inspect the Bureau in the South (instructions of April 7, first report May 8, 1866); they reported that many agents interfered 'arbitrarily' in planter-laborer relations and sat in freedmen's courts deciding land and family disputes, that some officers competed with planters by running plantations and sawmills, and that this produced bitterness between whites and freedpeople, and they recommended transferring Bureau duties to the army; the response must tie these reported agent practices and resentment to Dunning's claims about oppressive agents and white hostility (limits: Johnson, an opponent of the Bureau, appointed the commissioners and later historians describe the inquiry as meant to discredit the Bureau; the same report praised 'judicious' officers and found good order where agents did not interfere; do not credit a response that says the report condemned the whole Bureau or proved Dunning's 'diabolical device' description). (3) The Bureau's role in Black voting in 1867: after the Military Reconstruction Acts of March 1867 required Southern states to elect constitutional conventions with Black men voting, Bureau Circular No. 9 (May 1, 1867) said measures would be taken to inform freedmen entitled to register and urged them to disregard threats; the response must tie the Bureau's involvement in Black registration and voting to Dunning's claim that white Southerners saw the Bureau as an instrument of national control (limit: army commanders, not the Bureau, ran registration; do not credit a response that says Bureau agents registered the voters or ran the elections). Other accurate events or developments from 1865 to 1877 are accepted when they are specific, verifiable, not in the excerpt, and linked to Dunning's claim by the response's own explanation. Naming an event without connecting it to the interpretation earns 0.

rows.name: Part C

descriptors.0: The response gives no event, an inaccurate or out-of-period event, only repeats an event or claim already in the Du Bois excerpt, names an event without explaining how it supports Du Bois, or adds an outside fact that does not bear on his interpretation.
descriptors.1: The response adds a specific, accurate event or development from 1865 to 1877 that is not in the excerpts and explains how it supports Du Bois's interpretation.

rows.task_specific: Credit requires BOTH (a) one specific, accurate event or development from 1865 to 1877 that the excerpts do not mention (what happened, who acted, roughly when) AND (b) an explicit explanation of how that fact supports Du Bois's interpretation: the Bureau as an attempt to protect freed people's economic and civil rights, a great task accomplished, and a task repudiated. A response that only repeats what the Du Bois excerpt already says (that the Bureau met white opposition, that it was repudiated, or that its agents included teachers) earns 0; naming an event without explaining the link earns 0; adding a specific outside fact and explaining the link may earn 1. Examples with the connection each needs (not an exhaustive list): (1) The Black Codes of 1865-1866: in late 1865 legislatures such as Mississippi's and South Carolina's passed laws requiring freed workers to hold written yearly labor contracts, treating those without lawful employment as vagrants who could be fined and hired out, and restricting their rights in other ways; the response must tie the codes to the economic and civil rights Du Bois says the Bureau was meant to protect (limit: the codes show the need for protection, not that the Bureau succeeded). (2) Johnson's reversal of land policy, 1865-1866: Sherman's Special Field Order No. 15 (January 1865) had set aside coastal land in South Carolina and Georgia for freed families; after Johnson's amnesty and pardons, most of it, including land on Edisto Island, South Carolina, was returned to former owners in 1865-1866; the response must tie this to the national government's withdrawal of support for freed people's economic independence and so to Du Bois's judgment that the Bureau's work was repudiated (limit: Bureau officers themselves carried out the restoration; do not credit a response that says the Bureau opposed it). (3) Bureau support for Black colleges, credited only with an accurate role: the Fisk Free Colored School opened in Nashville in January 1866, founded by American Missionary Association representatives together with Bureau education superintendent John Ogden, and General Clinton B. Fisk helped secure former Union army hospital barracks for it; Howard University was chartered by Congress on March 2, 1867, was named for Bureau Commissioner O. O. Howard, who was one of its founders, and the Bureau helped fund its early campus (including a medical building and hospital in 1869); the response must tie the support to Du Bois's claim that the Bureau accomplished a great task (limits: do not credit a response that says the Bureau founded either college alone; the Du Bois excerpt already names Bureau teachers and educational leaders, so a general reference to Bureau schools, or to Cravath, earns 0). (4) The end of the Bureau: most of its work ended by 1868-1869 and Congress discontinued its remaining functions in 1872, while the rights of freed people were still contested; the response must tie this to Du Bois's judgment that the Bureau was repudiated (the end of the Bureau alone is not evidence that its work was a success). Other accurate events or developments from 1865 to 1877 are accepted when they are specific, verifiable, not in the excerpts, and linked to Du Bois's claim by the response's own explanation.

scoring_notes: Each part is worth one point. Parts are scored separately.
In part A, the difference must be about the two interpretations of the Bureau. Describing only one author, or a similarity, does not earn the point.

In parts B and C, the scoring turns on two questions. (i) Does the response add a specific outside fact (what happened, who, roughly when) that is not in the excerpts? Repeating an event or claim the excerpt already makes earns 0; adding a specific fact the excerpt does not contain may earn 1. (ii) Does the response explain how that fact supports THIS author's interpretation? A bare event name, or an event that merely happened in the Reconstruction period, earns 0. The events listed in the criteria are examples, not a complete list: accept any other accurate, specific, verifiable event or development from 1865 to 1877 that is not in the excerpts when the response explains how it fits the author's claim, and apply the conditions and limits stated for the listed examples.

Do not accept events that the excerpts already mention (for example Bureau agents who taught school in part C). Credit the Bureau's support for specific colleges only for the accurate role described in part C.

Dunning's account is one historian's 1907 interpretation; it reflects the racial prejudices of its time and has been widely criticized by later historians. Du Bois's article is also one historian's interpretation and was an early challenge to the Dunning view. Answers should describe the authors' interpretations without endorsing either.
ALTON practice rubric, not official College Board scoring: model scores are an ALTON estimate and no AP score is implied.

a: Dunning emphasizes that the Bureau's intrusion into Southern social life aroused violent hostility among white Southerners, while Du Bois emphasizes that it was an attempt to protect freed people's economic and civil rights.
Dunning points to ignorant or oppressive local agents, while Du Bois points to Bureau agents who were teachers and educational leaders.
Dunning describes how the Bureau looked to the white South (a device for humiliating whites), while Du Bois judges that the Bureau accomplished a great task and was repudiated.
b: Andrew Johnson vetoed the Freedmen's Bureau Bill on February 19, 1866, objecting that it would extend military jurisdiction over civilians in peacetime, with agents acting as judges without juries, in states that had no representation in Congress; this shows a contemporary view that the Bureau intruded into Southern life, which fits Dunning's claim.

In 1866 Generals Steedman and Fullerton, sent by President Johnson, reported that many Bureau agents interfered arbitrarily in relations between planters and laborers and that this bred bitterness between whites and freedpeople; this documents the agent conduct and hostility Dunning describes (though the inquiry was appointed by an opponent of the Bureau).

After Congress required Black men to vote in the constitutional conventions of 1867, the Bureau (Circular No. 9, May 1867) told freedmen how to register and to disregard threats; white Southerners who saw the Bureau backing Black voters could read it as an instrument of national political control, as Dunning says.
c: In late 1865 Southern legislatures such as Mississippi's and South Carolina's passed Black Codes that required freed workers to hold yearly written labor contracts and punished those without lawful employment as vagrants, which shows the need for the protection of economic and civil rights that Du Bois says the Bureau attempted.

In 1865 and 1866 President Johnson's amnesty and pardons led to the return of most of the land that Sherman's Field Order No. 15 had set aside for freed families, including land on Edisto Island, South Carolina; the national government's withdrawal of support for freed families' economic independence supports Du Bois's point that the Bureau's task was repudiated.

Howard University was chartered by Congress in 1867 and named for Bureau Commissioner O. O. Howard, and the Bureau helped fund its early campus; Bureau support for such institutions supports Du Bois's statement that the Bureau accomplished a great task.

Most of the Bureau's work had ended by 1868-1869 and Congress discontinued its remaining functions in 1872, while freed people's rights were still contested, which supports Du Bois's statement that the Bureau was repudiated.

common_pitfalls: Describing a similarity between the two excerpts instead of a difference.
Repeating something the excerpt already says (white hostility in part B; teachers who were Bureau agents or white opposition in part C) instead of adding a new fact.
Naming an event (for example the Black Codes) without saying how it supports the author.
Saying that Bureau agents registered Black voters, or that the Bureau alone founded Fisk or Howard University.
Assigning the Du Bois view to Dunning or the reverse.
facts: Congress created the Freedmen's Bureau on March 3, 1865, within the War Department; Oliver Otis Howard was appointed Commissioner in May 1865, and the Bureau was not abolished until 1872, though most of its work took place between June 1865 and December 1868.

President Andrew Johnson vetoed the Freedmen's Bureau Bill on February 19, 1866, objecting that it would extend military jurisdiction over civilians in peacetime, with agents acting as judges without juries, in eleven states without representation in Congress; the Senate failed to override that veto, and Congress overrode his veto of a second bill in July 1866.

Generals James Steedman and Joseph Fullerton, appointed by Johnson, inspected the Bureau in 1866 (instructions of April 7; first report May 8, 1866), criticized agents who interfered 'arbitrarily' in planter-laborer relations and officers who ran plantations and sawmills, praised 'judicious' officers, and recommended turning Bureau duties over to the army.

After the Military Reconstruction Acts of March 1867, Bureau Circular No. 9 (May 1, 1867) said measures would be taken to inform freedmen entitled to be registered and urged them to disregard threats; army commanders supervised registration.

In late 1865 the legislatures of Mississippi and South Carolina, among others, passed Black Codes that required written yearly labor contracts, treated the unemployed as vagrants, and limited freed people's rights.

General William T. Sherman's Special Field Order No. 15 (January 1865) set aside coastal land in South Carolina and Georgia for freed families; after Johnson's amnesty and pardons most of that land was returned to former owners in 1865-1866.

The Fisk Free Colored School opened in Nashville in January 1866, founded by American Missionary Association representatives (Edward P. Smith, Erastus M. Cravath) with Bureau education superintendent John Ogden; General Clinton B. Fisk helped secure former Union army hospital barracks for it.

Howard University was chartered by Congress on March 2, 1867, and named for Commissioner O. O. Howard, a founder; the Bureau helped fund its early campus and built a medical building and hospital there in 1869.

Historians of the Dunning school, named for William A. Dunning, portrayed Reconstruction as misgovernment; Du Bois challenged that view in Black Reconstruction in America (1935), and most historians abandoned the Dunning interpretation by the 1960s (Eric Foner).

samples.essay:

Dunning stresses how the Bureau's reach into Southern social life made white Southerners hostile and treats many local agents as unfit, while Du Bois treats the Bureau as a great task meant to protect freed people's economic and civil rights that the country abandoned too soon.

(B) One development that supports Dunning is President Andrew Johnson's veto of the Freedmen's Bureau Bill on February 19, 1866. Historical source (real document)
These sources are real historical sources (excerpts are cut verbatim from the repository text, with any OCR corrections listed in the credit line; [...] marks an omission).

(primary source)
Charter of Privileges Granted by William Penn to the Inhabitants of Pennsylvania and Territories (excerpt, Article I)
William Penn, Proprietary and Governor of Pennsylvania, 1701 (October 28). Avalon Project, Yale Law School (transcription). Reuse: public domain (published before 1929). excerpted (one contiguous passage, Article I up to its first sentence-ending clause); whitespace normalized; the transcription's apparent typo 'super' corrected to 'suffer' (the word the sentence requires); no other wording changed.
Context: Issued in 1701 by the owner and governor of the colony of Pennsylvania, which King Charles II had granted to him in 1681, at the request of the colony's Assembly.

"FIRST BECAUSE no People can be truly happy, though under the greatest Enjoyment of Civil Liberties, if abridged of the Freedom of their Consciences, as to their Religious Profession and Worship: And Almighty God being the only Lord of Conscience, Father of Lights and Spirits; and the Author as well as Object of all divine Knowledge, Faith and Worship, who only doth enlighten the Minds, and persuade and convince the Understandings of People, I do hereby grant and declare, That no Person or Persons, inhabiting in this Province or Territories, who shall confess and acknowledge One almighty God, the Creator, Upholder and Ruler of the World; and profess him or themselves obliged to live quietly under the Civil Government, shall be in any Case molested or prejudiced, in his or their Person or Estate, because of his or their conscientious Persuasion or Practice, nor be compelled to frequent or maintain any religious Worship, Place or Ministry, contrary to his or their Mind, or to do or suffer any other Act or Thing, contrary to their religious Persuasion."

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Briefly describe ONE right or protection that Penn grants to the inhabitants of Pennsylvania in the excerpt.
parts.model_answer: People who believe in one almighty God and live peaceably cannot be harassed or harmed in their persons or property because of their religious beliefs or practices.

rubric_rows.criterion: Describe one right or protection that the excerpt grants. Acceptable answers include: people who acknowledge one almighty God may not be molested or harmed in person or property because of their religious beliefs or practices; no inhabitant may be forced to attend or support any religious worship, place or ministry against his own mind.
required_elements: People who believe in one almighty God and live peaceably cannot be harassed or harmed in their persons or property because of their religious beliefs or practices.
No inhabitant can be forced to attend or pay for any religious worship or ministry against his own conscience.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE way that religious toleration such as Penn describes affected the settlement or society of Pennsylvania in the late 1600s and early 1700s.
parts.model_answer: Toleration attracted settlers of many faiths and nationalities, including German-speaking Mennonites and other Protestants and Scots-Irish Presbyterians, so Pennsylvania's population became more religiously and ethnically diverse than that of most colonies.

rubric_rows.criterion: Explain one specific, accurate effect of Pennsylvania's religious toleration on settlement or society in the late 1600s and early 1700s. Examples: it attracted settlers of many faiths and nationalities, including German-speaking Protestants such as Mennonites and Scots-Irish Presbyterians, so the population became unusually diverse; it helped Pennsylvania and its capital Philadelphia grow rapidly; it produced a society in which many denominations built churches side by side.
required_elements: Toleration attracted settlers of many faiths and nationalities, including German-speaking Mennonites and other Protestants and Scots-Irish Presbyterians, so Pennsylvania's population became more religiously and ethnically diverse than that of most colonies.
Because Pennsylvania offered freedom of conscience, many immigrants came, and the colony and Philadelphia grew quickly into a leading center of population and trade in British North America.
Quakers, Anglicans, Lutherans, Presbyterians, Baptists and others worshipped in separate congregations in Philadelphia and nearby towns, creating a society of religious pluralism.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE way that religious policy in another English colony in the 1600s differed from the policy described in the excerpt.
parts.model_answer: In Massachusetts Bay, Puritan leaders limited voting to church members for most of the 1600s and banished dissenters such as Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson, while Penn promised that people would not be punished for their religious beliefs.

rubric_rows.criterion: Explain one specific, accurate difference between the religious policy in another English colony in the 1600s and Penn's policy of toleration. Examples: Massachusetts Bay, where Puritan leaders restricted voting to church members for most of the 1600s, supported the Congregational church, and banished dissenters such as Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson; Massachusetts's execution of four Quakers between 1659 and 1661; Virginia's established Church of England supported by colonists' taxes.
required_elements: In Massachusetts Bay, Puritan leaders limited voting to church members for most of the 1600s and banished dissenters such as Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson, while Penn promised that people would not be punished for their religious beliefs.
Massachusetts hanged four Quakers between 1659 and 1661, whereas Penn, himself a Quaker, protected people from being harmed for their beliefs.

Virginia established the Church of England and required colonists to pay taxes to support its ministers, while Penn promised that no one would be forced to support a religious ministry against his mind.

Note: Each part is worth one point. Parts are scored separately.
Note: In part A, the response must describe a right the excerpt actually grants. Accept paraphrase. The excerpt does not itself grant the right to hold office or promise equal rights to non-Christians or people who deny God, so do not credit those.
Note: In part B, the effect must be tied to Pennsylvania's toleration. A bare statement that Pennsylvania grew does not earn the point unless it is connected to toleration.
Note: In part C, the colony and the difference must both be specific. A bare claim that another tolerant colony (for example Rhode Island) was also tolerant does not show a difference; a response that names a specific, accurate difference in policy may earn the point.

Acceptable answers for A: People who believe in one almighty God and live peaceably cannot be harassed or harmed in their persons or property because of their religious beliefs or practices. / No inhabitant can be forced to attend or pay for any religious worship or ministry against his own conscience.
Acceptable answers for B: Toleration attracted settlers of many faiths and nationalities, including German-speaking Mennonites and other Protestants and Scots-Irish Presbyterians, so Pennsylvania's population became more religiously and ethnically diverse than that of most colonies. / Because Pennsylvania offered freedom of conscience, many immigrants came, and the colony and Philadelphia grew quickly into a leading center of population and trade in British North America. / Quakers, Anglicans, Lutherans, Presbyterians, Baptists and others worshipped in separate congregations in Philadelphia and nearby towns, creating a society of religious pluralism.

Sample response, high score (3/3; Part A 1, Part B 1, Part C 1):
(A) One right Penn grants is that people who acknowledge one almighty God and live peacefully cannot be harassed or harmed in their persons or property because of their religious beliefs or practices.

(B) Toleration drew settlers of many faiths and nationalities to Pennsylvania. German-speaking Mennonites and other Protestants came, along with Scots-Irish Presbyterians, so by the early 1700s Pennsylvania's population was more religiously and ethnically mixed than the populations of most other colonies.

(C) In Massachusetts Bay, Puritan leaders allowed only church members to vote for most of the century and used banishment against dissenters such as Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson. Penn's charter, by contrast, protects people from being harmed for their religious practice and says no one can be forced to support a ministry against his own mind.
   - "people who acknowledge one almighty God and live peacefully cannot be harassed or harmed" - Accurately paraphrases the protection granted in the excerpt, including its condition. Earns the Part A point.
   - "German-speaking Mennonites and other Protestants came" - Specific, accurate evidence of who toleration attracted.
   - "more religiously and ethnically mixed than the populations of most other colonies" - Ties the effect directly to toleration and to the society of the colony. Earns the Part B point.
   - "used banishment against dissenters such as Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson" - Names a specific, accurate Massachusetts policy and contrasts it with Penn's policy. Earns the Part C point.

Sample response, middle score (2/3; Part A 1, Part B 1, Part C 0):
(A) Penn says that nobody who believes in one almighty God can be hurt or punished because of his religion, and nobody can be forced to go to a church he does not agree with.

(B) Penn's charter helped Pennsylvania a lot. Pennsylvania grew and became an important colony because of the charter.

(C) Massachusetts Bay was run by Puritans who required people to be church members to vote for most of the 1600s. Dissenters such as Roger Williams were banished, which is very different from Penn's promise that people would not be harmed for their beliefs.
   - "nobody who believes in one almighty God can be hurt or punished because of his religion" - Accurately describes a protection granted in the excerpt. Earns the Part A point.
   - "Pennsylvania grew and became an important colony because of the charter" - A vague claim that does not explain how toleration affected settlement or society. No credit for Part B.
   - "required people to be church members to vote for most of the 1600s" - Specific, accurate Massachusetts policy that differs from Penn's. Earns the Part C point.

Sample response, low score (1/3; Part A 1, Part B 0, Part C 0):
(A) Penn gives the people of Pennsylvania the right to practice their religion without being harmed because of what they believe.

(B) Religion was important to the colonists in Pennsylvania and the charter made them happy and helped the colony.

(C) Other colonies had different religions and some of them were not as friendly to other religions as Pennsylvania was.
   - "the right to practice their religion without being harmed because of what they believe" - Accurately describes a protection in the excerpt. Earns the Part A point.
   - "the charter made them happy and helped the colony" - Names no specific effect and does not explain how toleration shaped settlement or society. No credit for Part B.
   - "some of them were not as friendly to other religions as Pennsylvania was" - Names no colony and no specific policy, so it does not show a specific difference. No credit for Part C.

sources.body: FIRST BECAUSE no People can be truly happy, though under the greatest Enjoyment of Civil Liberties, if abridged of the Freedom of their Consciences, as to their Religious Profession and Worship: And Almighty God being the only Lord of Conscience, Father of Lights and Spirits; and the Author as well as Object of all divine Knowledge, Faith and Worship, who only doth enlighten the Minds, and persuade and convince the Understandings of People, I do hereby grant and declare, That no Person or Persons, inhabiting in this Province or Territories, who shall confess and acknowledge One almighty God, the Creator, Upholder and Ruler of the World; and profess him or themselves obliged to live quietly under the Civil Government, shall be in any Case molested or prejudiced, in his or their Person or Estate, because of his or their conscientious Persuasion or Practice, nor be compelled to frequent or maintain any religious Worship, Place or Ministry, contrary to his or their Mind, or to do or suffer any other Act or Thing, contrary to their religious Persuasion.

rows.name: Part A

descriptors.0: The response misreads the excerpt, gives a right the excerpt does not grant, or is too vague to show what the excerpt says.
descriptors.1: The response accurately describes one right or protection granted in the excerpt.

rows.task_specific: Describe one right or protection that the excerpt grants. Acceptable answers include: people who acknowledge one almighty God may not be molested or harmed in person or property because of their religious beliefs or practices; no inhabitant may be forced to attend or support any religious worship, place or ministry against his own mind.

rows.name: Part B

descriptors.0: The response gives no effect, an inaccurate effect, or one from the wrong period, or does not explain how toleration produced it.
descriptors.1: The response explains how toleration produced one specific, accurate effect on settlement or society in Pennsylvania in the late 1600s and early 1700s.

rows.task_specific: Explain one specific, accurate effect of Pennsylvania's religious toleration on settlement or society in the late 1600s and early 1700s. Examples: it attracted settlers of many faiths and nationalities, including German-speaking Protestants such as Mennonites and Scots-Irish Presbyterians, so the population became unusually diverse; it helped Pennsylvania and its capital Philadelphia grow rapidly; it produced a society in which many denominations built churches side by side.

rows.name: Part C

descriptors.0: The response gives no colony, an inaccurate difference, or a colony outside the period, or does not explain how it differed from Penn's policy.
descriptors.1: The response explains one specific, accurate difference between another English colony's religious policy in the 1600s and Penn's policy.

rows.task_specific: Explain one specific, accurate difference between the religious policy in another English colony in the 1600s and Penn's policy of toleration. Examples: Massachusetts Bay, where Puritan leaders restricted voting to church members for most of the 1600s, supported the Congregational church, and banished dissenters such as Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson; Massachusetts's execution of four Quakers between 1659 and 1661; Virginia's established Church of England supported by colonists' taxes.

scoring_notes: Each part is worth one point. Parts are scored separately.

In part A, the response must describe a right the excerpt actually grants. Accept paraphrase. The excerpt does not itself grant the right to hold office or promise equal rights to non-Christians or people who deny God, so do not credit those.
In part B, the effect must be tied to Pennsylvania's toleration. A bare statement that Pennsylvania grew does not earn the point unless it is connected to toleration.

In part C, the colony and the difference must both be specific. A bare claim that another tolerant colony (for example Rhode Island) was also tolerant does not show a difference; a response that names a specific, accurate difference in policy may earn the point.
ALTON practice rubric, not official College Board scoring: model scores are an ALTON estimate and no AP score is implied.

a: People who believe in one almighty God and live peaceably cannot be harassed or harmed in their persons or property because of their religious beliefs or practices.
No inhabitant can be forced to attend or pay for any religious worship or ministry against his own conscience.
b: Toleration attracted settlers of many faiths and nationalities, including German-speaking Mennonites and other Protestants and Scots-Irish Presbyterians, so Pennsylvania's population became more religiously and ethnically diverse than that of most colonies.
Because Pennsylvania offered freedom of conscience, many immigrants came, and the colony and Philadelphia grew quickly into a leading center of population and trade in British North America.
Quakers, Anglicans, Lutherans, Presbyterians, Baptists and others worshipped in separate congregations in Philadelphia and nearby towns, creating a society of religious pluralism.
c: In Massachusetts Bay, Puritan leaders limited voting to church members for most of the 1600s and banished dissenters such as Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson, while Penn promised that people would not be punished for their religious beliefs.
Massachusetts hanged four Quakers between 1659 and 1661, whereas Penn, himself a Quaker, protected people from being harmed for their beliefs.

Virginia established the Church of England and required colonists to pay taxes to support its ministers, while Penn promised that no one would be forced to support a religious ministry against his mind.

common_pitfalls: Saying the charter granted religious freedom to everyone: the excerpt protects those who acknowledge one almighty God and live peaceably.
Naming Massachusetts or Virginia without saying how its policy differed.
Giving an effect from the eighteenth century far beyond 1701 as the main example.
Confusing the 1701 charter with the 1681 royal charter.
facts: King Charles II granted Pennsylvania to William Penn in 1681.
Penn was a Quaker and issued the Charter of Privileges in 1701.
Germantown, near Philadelphia, was founded in 1683 by German-speaking settlers.
Massachusetts Bay restricted the vote to church members for most of the 1600s; the charter of 1691 replaced the church test with a property qualification.
Roger Williams was banished from Massachusetts Bay in 1635 and Anne Hutchinson in 1637-1638.
Massachusetts executed four Quakers between 1659 and 1661.
Virginia established the Church of England and supported it with parish taxes.

(B) Toleration drew settlers of many faiths and nationalities to Pennsylvania. (C) In Massachusetts Bay, Puritan leaders allowed only church members to vote for most of the century and used banishment against dissenters such as Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson. Penn's charter, by contrast, protects people from being harmed for their religious practice and says no one can be forced to support a ministry against his own mind.

Part A (0-1): Describe one condition of 1930s farm families that the photograph or its title reflects, such as destitution, migrant farm labor, or displacement in search of work.
   - 1: The response accurately describes one condition of 1930s farm families that the photograph or its title reflects.
   - 0: The response misreads the photograph, gives a vague statement, or names no condition that the photograph and title reflect.
Part B (0-1): Explain one specific cause of 1930s farm hardship, such as collapsing crop prices in the Great Depression, drought and dust storms in the Dust Bowl, or the displacement of tenant farmers and sharecroppers.
   - 1: The response explains how one specific, accurate historical development caused the hardship of 1930s farm families.
   - 0: The response gives no cause, gives a cause from the wrong period, or does not explain how the cause produced the hardship.
Part C (0-1): Explain one specific federal response to 1930s farm hardship, such as the Agricultural Adjustment Act, the Resettlement Administration or Farm Security Administration, or other New Deal relief for rural Americans.
   - 1: The response explains one specific, accurate federal response to the hardship of 1930s farm families.
   - 0: The response gives no federal response, an inaccurate or out-of-period one, or does not explain what it did.
Note: Each part is worth one point. Parts are scored separately.
Note: In part A, accept a condition that the photograph or its title shows. Students do not need to name the photographer or the family.
Note: In part B, a bare name such as 'the Dust Bowl' with no explanation of how it produced hardship does not earn the point.
Note: In part C, accept federal programs that aided farm families or rural workers in the 1930s if the response says what the program did.

Acceptable answers for C: The Resettlement Administration (1935) and its successor the Farm Security Administration (1937) lent money to poor farmers and ran camps for migrant farm workers. / The Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1933 paid farmers to reduce production in order to raise crop prices. / The Resettlement Administration and the Farm Security Administration employed photographers such as the one who took this picture to document rural poverty and build support for relief.

Sample response, high score (3/3; Part A 1, Part B 1, Part C 1):
(A) One condition shown is that many farm families in the 1930s were so poor that they became migrant laborers. The title calls the people 'destitute pea pickers,' which shows a family traveling from crop to crop and living in poverty.

(B) One cause was the Great Depression, which collapsed crop prices after 1929. Farmers who could not sell their crops for enough to pay their debts or rent lost their land or work, and many of them turned to seasonal farm labor in places like California.

(C) One response was the Resettlement Administration, created in 1935 and replaced by the Farm Security Administration in 1937. These agencies lent money to poor farmers and built camps for migrant farm workers, and they hired photographers to document rural poverty.
   - "many farm families in the 1930s were so poor that they became migrant laborers" - Describes an accurate condition and ties it to the photograph's title ('destitute pea pickers'). Earns the Part A point.
   - "the Great Depression, which collapsed crop prices after 1929" - Names a specific, accurate cause.
   - "Farmers who could not sell their crops for enough to pay their debts or rent lost their land or work" - Explains how the cause produced the hardship. Earns the Part B point.
   - "lent money to poor farmers and built camps for migrant farm workers" - Specific, accurate description of what the federal agencies did. Earns the Part C point.

Sample response, middle score (2/3; Part A 1, Part B 1, Part C 0):
(A) The photograph shows that many farm families in the 1930s were very poor and had to travel to find work. The title says that the woman and her children were destitute pea pickers.

(B) The people in the picture were struggling because of the hard times in the country. Everything was difficult for farmers then.

(C) The Resettlement Administration helped poor farmers by giving them loans and building camps for people who traveled to work on farms, and later it became the Farm Security Administration.
   - "many farm families in the 1930s were very poor and had to travel to find work" - Accurate condition drawn from the photograph and its title. Earns the Part A point.
   - "because of the hard times in the country" - Too vague. It names no specific cause such as falling crop prices or the Dust Bowl. No credit for Part B.
   - "giving them loans and building camps for people who traveled to work on farms" - Specific, accurate federal response. Earns the Part C point.

Sample response, low score (1/3; Part A 1, Part B 0, Part C 0):
(A) The photograph shows a poor mother with her children. The title says they were destitute and that they picked peas in California.

(B) The family had a hard life because things were difficult in the 1930s and not many people had money.

(C) The government tried to help people during the 1930s by creating programs, and many people were thankful.
   - "The title says they were destitute and that they picked peas in California" - Accurately reads the title and the condition it reflects. Earns the Part A point.
   - "things were difficult in the 1930s and not many people had money" - Restates the hardship and names no specific cause. No credit for Part B.
   - "The government tried to help people during the 1930s by creating programs" - Names no specific program or what it did. No credit for Part C.

payload.set_intro:
Historical source (real document)
These documents are real historical sources (excerpts are cut verbatim from the repository text; [...] marks an omission). Document 7 is an image shown below the documents.

Document 1 (primary source)
Executive Order 9835, Prescribing Procedures for the Administration of an Employees Loyalty Program in the Executive Branch of the Government (excerpts)
Harry S. Truman, President of the United States, 1947 (March 21). Harry S. Truman Library and Museum (National Archives and Records Administration). Reuse: public domain (U.S. government work). excerpted (three segments joined by [...]: part of the preamble, the first provision of the order on applicants, and the clause on membership in organizations from the section on standards); whitespace normalized; no wording changed.
Context: An order signed by the President on March 21, 1947, setting up loyalty investigations of federal employees; the segments below are part of the preamble, the first provision of the order on job applicants, and a clause from the section describing evidence that may be considered in judging disloyalty.

"WHEREAS, although the loyalty of by far the overwhelming majority of all Government employees is beyond question, the presence within the Government service of any disloyal or subversive person constitutes a threat to our democratic processes; and WHEREAS maximum protection must be afforded the United States against infiltration of disloyal persons into the ranks of its employees, and equal protection from unfounded accusations of disloyalty must be afforded the loyal employees of the Government: [...] There shall be a loyalty investigation of every person entering the civilian employment of any department or agency of the executive branch of the Federal Government. [...] Membership in, affiliation with or sympathetic association with any foreign or domestic organization, association, movement, group or combination of persons, designated by the Attorney General as totalitarian, fascist, communist, or subversive, or as having adopted a policy of advocating or approving the commission of acts of force or violence to deny persons their rights under the Constitution of the United States, or as seeking to alter the form of government of the United States by unconstitutional means."

———

Document 2 (primary source)
Declaration of Conscience (excerpts)
Margaret Chase Smith, U.S. Senator from Maine (Republican), 1950 (June 1). U.S. Senate, Office of Art & History (from the Congressional Record, 81st Congress, 2nd Session). Between 1947 and 1962, rivalry with the Soviet Union shaped American politics and everyday life. The United States built a large peacetime military, investigated the loyalty of federal employees, and prepared for the possibility of nuclear attack. Americans argued over whether these measures protected the nation or threatened its freedoms.

Evaluate the extent to which fear of the Soviet Union and communism shaped American government policy and public life from 1947 to 1962.

In your response you should do the following:
- Respond to the prompt with a historically defensible thesis or claim that establishes a line of reasoning.
- Describe a broader historical context relevant to the prompt.
- Support an argument in response to the prompt using at least four documents.
- Use at least one additional piece of specific historical evidence (beyond that found in the documents) relevant to an argument about the prompt.
- For at least two documents, explain how or why the document's point of view, purpose, historical situation, and/or audience is relevant to an argument.
- Demonstrate a complex understanding of the historical development that is the focus of the prompt, using evidence to corroborate, qualify, or modify an argument that addresses the question.

After World War II the wartime alliance between the United States and the Soviet Union collapsed as Soviet power spread across Eastern Europe. In March 1947 President Truman asked Congress for aid to Greece and Turkey, and containment became the framework for American foreign policy. In 1949 the Soviets tested an atomic bomb, communists won the civil war in China, and in June 1950 the Korean War began. Fear of the Soviet Union and communism shaped American government policy to a great extent between 1947 and 1962, producing loyalty programs, civil defense planning, a permanent military establishment and a new federal role in education. Its effect on public life was more contested, because the fear rested partly on real Soviet actions and because Americans, including officeholders, openly criticized the measures taken in its name.

The documents show fear reshaping what the federal government did. In Document 1, President Truman's 1947 order requires a loyalty investigation of every person entering civilian federal employment and lists "sympathetic association" with groups designated by the Attorney General as subversive among the evidence that may be considered. In Document 3, a federal board prepares citizens for atomic attack and urges them to learn the steps they can take to survive. Document 4, the findings of the National Defense Education Act, says that "the security of the Nation requires the fullest development of the mental resources and technical skills of its young men and women," tying schools to defense after Sputnik. Document 5 shows the budget consequences: national defense outlays rose from 13.7 billion dollars in 1950 to 46.1 billion in 1952 and took more than half of all federal spending in every year shown from 1952 through 1960. Together these documents show a government that organized its workforce, its civil preparedness, its schools and its budget around the Soviet threat.

Document 5 also qualifies the claim that fear alone explains policy. Defense outlays were only 9.1 billion dollars in 1948 and 13.7 billion in 1950, even though the Cold War was already under way, and they jumped after the Korean War began in June 1950. Because the table is a modern compilation of figures that shows spending and not motives, it cannot separate fear of the Soviet Union from the needs of a particular war. I would therefore say that fear helped keep spending high after Korea, but a specific war produced the largest increase.

Fear also reached public life, but the evidence is mixed. In Document 2, Senator Margaret Chase Smith describes "a national feeling of fear and frustration" and says that Americans were "afraid to speak their minds" for fear of being smeared as Communists or Fascists. That supports the claim that fear narrowed debate. However, she was a Republican senator rebuking a fellow Republican, Joseph McCarthy, in the Senate four months after his Wheeling speech, so her speech also shows that dissent was possible, and as a moderate speaking in a political dispute she may emphasize fear more than ordinary citizens did. Events outside the documents fit her warning: the House Un-American Activities Committee's 1947 hearings on Hollywood led to the blacklisting of the Hollywood Ten, and the Senate censured McCarthy in 1954, which shows both the reach of suspicion and its limits. In Document 6, President Eisenhower, a former general who had overseen much of the buildup and who was leaving office with no election to face, warns about "unwarranted influence" of the military-industrial complex, yet he also calls the buildup an imperative need and urges "an alert and knowledgeable citizenry." His farewell setting gives the warning weight, and it shows that public argument over the response never ended.

Finally, the fear was not only imagined. Document 7 is a reconnaissance photograph of a Soviet missile launch site in Cuba taken on October 14, 1962, with trailers and equipment labeled by government analysts. The government used photographs like this to persuade the public and other nations that the threat was real, so the image is both evidence and persuasion, and it shows equipment, not Soviet intentions. Still, the missiles were ninety miles from Florida, and the crisis that followed, which was resolved on October 28, helps explain why civil defense drills and shelters seemed reasonable to many Americans.

In sum, fear of the Soviet Union reshaped government policy to a great extent, but its effect on public life was limited by open criticism, by the role of specific events such as Korea and Sputnik, and by real Soviet capabilities that made some of the fear reasonable.

- Fear of the Soviet Union changed what the federal government did: loyalty programs, civil defense, military spending and education policy. Supports: Document 1, 3, 4, 5. Complicates: Document 2, 6.

Supports the claim that American fear had a basis in real Soviet weapons close to the United States and helps explain the peak of public anxiety in October 1962; it cannot show Soviet intentions. Sourcing: Taken by a U.S. reconnaissance aircraft and labeled by government analysts. The government used photographs like this to persuade the American public and other nations that the threat was real, so the image is evidence of a threat and also an instrument of persuasion; it takes interpretation to read an aerial photograph.

defensible_theses: Fear of the Soviet Union and communism shaped American government policy to a great extent between 1947 and 1962, producing loyalty programs, civil defense planning, a permanent military establishment and a new federal role in education, though specific events such as the Korean War and Sputnik drove many decisions and some leaders limited the response.

Fear shaped public life less completely than it shaped government: Americans such as Margaret Chase Smith and Dwight Eisenhower openly criticized loyalty politics and the growth of the military, and Congress insisted that states keep control of education, so the extent of change was real but contested.

The fear was part overreaction (loyalty investigations of employees, reassuring civil defense booklets) and part reasonable response to real Soviet capabilities (the 1949 atomic bomb, Sputnik, missiles in Cuba), so judging the extent to which fear shaped policy requires separating proportionate from excessive responses.

doc_uses.usable_for: Shows the federal government ordering a loyalty investigation of every person entering civilian federal employment and treating 'sympathetic association' with groups the Attorney General designated as subversive as evidence of disloyalty. Supports claims that fear reshaped government security policy and civil liberties; the preamble's statement that the loyalty of 'the overwhelming majority' of employees was 'beyond question' and its promise of 'equal protection from unfounded accusations' show the order presented itself as limited.
doc_uses.sourcing: An executive order issued by President Truman nine days after he asked Congress for aid to Greece and Turkey, and after Republicans won control of Congress in the 1946 elections while campaigning against communism in government. It is an official act that presents the program as protecting both the nation and the accused, so it shows how the administration wanted the policy seen.

doc_uses.usable_for: Describes 'a national feeling of fear and frustration' and says Americans were 'afraid to speak their minds' for fear of being smeared as Communists or Fascists. Supports claims that fear narrowed debate and encouraged suspicion; it also shows a senator publicly criticizing how the fear was used, which qualifies claims about the whole government.
doc_uses.sourcing: A speech to the Senate by a Republican senator from Maine, rebuking the tactics of a fellow Republican four months after his Wheeling speech. She was a moderate speaking as a public figure in a political dispute, so she may emphasize fear and unfairness more than ordinary citizens expressed; her willingness to speak shows that dissent was possible.

doc_uses.usable_for: Tells the public that its chances of living through an atomic attack are 'much better than you may have thought' and urges readers to learn 'the steps you can take.' Supports claims that the government planned for nuclear war and tried to manage public fear.
doc_uses.sourcing: Issued by a federal board in 1950 whose purpose was to prepare citizens and encourage civil defense planning. It aims to reduce panic and win support for preparation, so it downplays the dangers (it says even hydrogen bombs could not 'kill us all'); its audience is ordinary citizens, a year after the Soviets tested an atomic bomb.

doc_uses.usable_for: Declares that 'the security of the Nation requires the fullest development of the mental resources and technical skills of its young men and women' and links education to 'the defense of this Nation.' Supports claims that fear of Soviet technical advances reshaped education policy; its statement that states and local communities 'must retain control over and primary responsibility for public education' qualifies how far federal power grew.
doc_uses.sourcing: Congress's own statement of purpose, written to justify federal money for schools, which many had opposed as federal control of education. Framing the law as national defense helped build a majority after Sputnik, so the findings reflect a purpose of persuasion as well as fear.

doc_uses.usable_for: Shows national defense outlays of 9,105 million dollars in 1948 and 13,724 million in 1950, then 46,089 million in 1952, never below 42,523 million in the years shown after that, and more than half of all federal outlays in every year shown from 1952 to 1960 (49.0 percent in 1962). Supports claims that military priorities dominated the budget; the low 1948 and 1950 figures show that spending stayed low in the first Cold War years before the Korean War began.
doc_uses.sourcing: Official figures compiled in a later budget publication, so there is no persuasive purpose in the numbers, but they show spending and not motives. The jump coincides with the Korean War, so the table cannot by itself separate fear of the Soviet Union from the needs of a particular war; the figures are in current dollars and are not adjusted for inflation.

doc_uses.usable_for: Warns that 'this conjunction of an immense military establishment and a large arms industry is new in the American experience,' with influence 'felt in every city, every State house, every office of the Federal government,' yet recognizes 'the imperative need for this development.' Supports claims that Cold War fear transformed the economy and government; his call for 'an alert and knowledgeable citizenry' qualifies claims that fear silenced debate.
doc_uses.sourcing: A farewell address by a Republican president who was a former general and had overseen much of the buildup, speaking to the nation as he left office with no election to face. His experience gives the warning weight, and the farewell setting invites a reflective tone; he also affirms the need for defense, so he is not simply a critic.

doc_uses.usable_for: Shows a Soviet medium-range missile site in Cuba, with analysts' labels for tents, equipment, a convoy and six missile trailers. Supports the claim that American fear had a basis in real Soviet weapons close to the United States and helps explain the peak of public anxiety in October 1962; it cannot show Soviet intentions.
doc_uses.sourcing: Taken by a U.S. reconnaissance aircraft and labeled by government analysts. The government used photographs like this to persuade the American public and other nations that the threat was real, so the image is evidence of a threat and also an instrument of persuasion; it takes interpretation to read an aerial photograph.

samples.essay:
After World War II the wartime alliance between the United States and the Soviet Union collapsed as Soviet power spread across Eastern Europe. In March 1947 President Truman asked Congress for aid to Greece and Turkey, and containment became the framework for American foreign policy. In 1949 the Soviets tested an atomic bomb, communists won the civil war in China, and in June 1950 the Korean War began. Fear of the Soviet Union and communism shaped American government policy to a great extent between 1947 and 1962, producing loyalty programs, civil defense planning, a permanent military establishment and a new federal role in education. Its effect on public life was more contested, because the fear rested partly on real Soviet actions and because Americans, including officeholders, openly criticized the measures taken in its name.

The documents show fear reshaping what the federal government did. In Document 1, President Truman's 1947 order requires a loyalty investigation of every person entering civilian federal employment and lists "sympathetic association" with groups designated by the Attorney General as subversive among the evidence that may be considered. In Document 3, a federal board prepares citizens for atomic attack and urges them to learn the steps they can take to survive. Document 4, the findings of the National Defense Education Act, says that "the security of the Nation requires the fullest development of the mental resources and technical skills of its young men and women," tying schools to defense after Sputnik. Document 5 shows the budget consequences: national defense outlays rose from 13.7 billion dollars in 1950 to 46.1 billion in 1952 and took more than half of all federal spending in every year shown from 1952 through 1960. Together these documents show a government that organized its workforce, its civil preparedness, its schools and its budget around the Soviet threat.

Document 5 also qualifies the claim that fear alone explains policy. Defense outlays were only 9.1 billion dollars in 1948 and 13.7 billion in 1950, even though the Cold War was already under way, and they jumped after the Korean War began in June 1950. Because the table is a modern compilation of figures that shows spending and not motives, it cannot separate fear of the Soviet Union from the needs of a particular war. I would therefore say that fear helped keep spending high after Korea, but a specific war produced the largest increase.

Fear also reached public life, but the evidence is mixed. In Document 2, Senator Margaret Chase Smith describes "a national feeling of fear and frustration" and says that Americans were "afraid to speak their minds" for fear of being smeared as Communists or Fascists. That supports the claim that fear narrowed debate. However, she was a Republican senator rebuking a fellow Republican, Joseph McCarthy, in the Senate four months after his Wheeling speech, so her speech also shows that dissent was possible, and as a moderate speaking in a political dispute she may emphasize fear more than ordinary citizens did. Events outside the documents fit her warning: the House Un-American Activities Committee's 1947 hearings on Hollywood led to the blacklisting of the Hollywood Ten, and the Senate censured McCarthy in 1954, which shows both the reach of suspicion and its limits. In Document 6, President Eisenhower, a former general who had overseen much of the buildup and who was leaving office with no election to face, warns about "unwarranted influence" of the military-industrial complex, yet he also calls the buildup an imperative need and urges "an alert and knowledgeable citizenry." His farewell setting gives the warning weight, and it shows that public argument over the response never ended.

Finally, the fear was not only imagined. Document 7 is a reconnaissance photograph of a Soviet missile launch site in Cuba taken on October 14, 1962, with trailers and equipment labeled by government analysts. The government used photographs like this to persuade the public and other nations that the threat was real, so the image is both evidence and persuasion, and it shows equipment, not Soviet intentions. Still, the missiles were ninety miles from Florida, and the crisis that followed, which was resolved on October 28, helps explain why civil defense drills and shelters seemed reasonable to many Americans.

In sum, fear of the Soviet Union reshaped government policy to a great extent, but its effect on public life was limited by open criticism, by the role of specific events such as Korea and Sputnik, and by real Soviet capabilities that made some of the fear reasonable.
